BEGINNER1. What is an Event?

An event is a signal that something happened — a user clicked, typed, scrolled, submitted a form, or the page finished loading. JavaScript lets you "listen" for these signals and react to them.

Real-world analogy: Events are like a fire alarm system. When something happens in one room (the target), the alarm fires there first, then travels up through the building — floor alarm, building alarm. That's bubbling.

Common Event Types

  • Mouse: click, dblclick, mouseover, mouseout
  • Keyboard: keydown, keyup
  • Form: submit, input, change, focus, blur
  • Window: load, resize, scroll, DOMContentLoaded

BEGINNER2. addEventListener

addEventListener(type, handler) registers a function to run when an event fires. Always use it instead of assigning to onclick — addEventListener allows MULTIPLE handlers on the same element.

const btn = document.querySelector("#btn");

btn.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log("Button clicked!");
});

// Multiple listeners on the SAME event — both run
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("First handler"));
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("Second handler"));
// Clicking logs BOTH lines
❌ onclick — overwrites previous handlers: 
btn.onclick = () => console.log("A");
btn.onclick = () => console.log("B");
// Only "B" ever runs — "A" is GONE
✅ addEventListener — stacks handlers: 
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("A"));
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("B"));
// Both "A" and "B" run

BEGINNER3. The Event Object

Every handler automatically receives an event object describing what happened.

document.querySelector("#btn").addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    console.log(e.target);        // the exact element that was clicked
    console.log(e.currentTarget); // the element the listener is attached to
    console.log(e.type);          // "click"
});

document.querySelector("input").addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
    console.log(e.key);      // e.g. "Enter", "Escape", "a"
    console.log(e.code);     // e.g. "Enter", "KeyA" — physical key, layout-independent
    if (e.key === "Enter") {
        console.log("Enter was pressed");
    }
});
💡 Tip: e.target and e.currentTarget are often the SAME element, but not always — target is where the event originated, currentTarget is where the listener you're inside was attached. This matters a lot for event delegation (Section 7).

INTERMEDIATE4. preventDefault()

Many events have a built-in browser DEFAULT action — following a link, submitting a form and reloading the page. e.preventDefault() cancels that default so you can handle it yourself.

const form = document.querySelector("form");

form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault(); // stops the page from reloading
    const data = new FormData(form);
    console.log("Submitting via JS instead:", Object.fromEntries(data));
    // ... send data with fetch() instead of a full page reload
});

// Also common on links
document.querySelector("a.tab-link").addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault(); // don't navigate away
    showTab(e.target.dataset.tab);
});

INTERMEDIATE5. Event Bubbling & Capturing

Most events travel through THREE phases: capturing (top-down, from document to the target), the target phase, then bubbling (bottom-up, back to document). By default, listeners fire during the bubbling phase.

<div id="outer">
    <button id="inner">Click me</button>
</div>

document.querySelector("#outer").addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log("outer div handler");
});
document.querySelector("#inner").addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log("inner button handler");
});

// Clicking the button logs BOTH, in this order (bubbling — inside out):
// "inner button handler"
// "outer div handler"

Capturing Phase

// Pass { capture: true } to listen during the DOWNWARD (capturing) phase instead
document.querySelector("#outer").addEventListener(
    "click",
    () => console.log("outer (capturing)"),
    { capture: true }
);
// This would fire BEFORE the inner button's bubbling-phase handler

INTERMEDIATE6. stopPropagation()

e.stopPropagation() stops an event from continuing its journey through the bubbling (or capturing) phases — ancestor listeners further along the path will NOT fire.

const outer = document.querySelector("#outer");
const inner = document.querySelector("#inner");

outer.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("outer clicked"));
inner.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    console.log("inner clicked");
    e.stopPropagation(); // outer's handler will NOT run
});

// Clicking #inner now only logs:
// "inner clicked"
⚠️ Use Sparingly: Overusing stopPropagation() can break event delegation patterns elsewhere in your app that rely on bubbling to a common ancestor. Only stop propagation when you have a specific reason to isolate the event.

ADVANCED7. Event Delegation

Event delegation exploits bubbling: instead of attaching a listener to every child element, attach ONE listener to a shared parent and inspect e.target to determine what was actually clicked. This automatically works for elements added LATER, too.

const list = document.querySelector("ul");

// One listener handles clicks on ALL current AND future 
  •  elements
list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    if (!e.target.matches("li")) return; // ignore clicks that aren't on an 
  • 
    e.target.classList.toggle("done");
    console.log("Toggled:", e.target.textContent);
});

// New items added later are automatically handled — no extra listeners needed!
const newItem = document.createElement("li");
newItem.textContent = "New task";
list.append(newItem);
    • Why this matters: Attaching a listener directly to a dynamically-created element only works if you remember to re-attach it every time. Delegation on a stable parent means you register the listener ONCE and never worry about it again.

    ADVANCED8. Removing Listeners

    removeEventListener requires the EXACT SAME function reference used in addEventListener — an inline arrow function or anonymous function can never be removed because there's no way to refer back to it.

    // ❌ Cannot be removed — no reference was kept
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("clicked"));
// btn.removeEventListener("click", () => console.log("clicked")); // does NOTHING — different function!

// ✅ Store the function in a variable to remove it later
function handleClick() {
    console.log("clicked");
}
btn.addEventListener("click", handleClick);
btn.removeEventListener("click", handleClick); // works — same reference

// { once: true } — auto-removes the listener after it fires ONE time
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("only once"), { once: true });

    ADVANCED9. Common Pitfalls

    1. Using onclick Instead of addEventListener

    // ❌ Only one handler can ever exist — later assignments silently replace earlier ones
el.onclick = handlerA;
el.onclick = handlerB; // handlerA is gone!

// ✅ addEventListener lets multiple parts of code listen independently
el.addEventListener("click", handlerA);
el.addEventListener("click", handlerB);

    2. Forgetting preventDefault on Forms

    // ❌ Page reloads, losing all JS state, before your handler even finishes
form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
    sendData(); // too late — page is already navigating away
});

// ✅ Prevent default FIRST
form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    sendData();
});

    3. Attaching a New Listener to Every List Item

    // ❌ Doesn't scale, and misses items added later
document.querySelectorAll("li").forEach(li => {
    li.addEventListener("click", handleClick);
});

// ✅ Delegate to the parent instead (see Section 7)
document.querySelector("ul").addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    if (e.target.matches("li")) handleClick(e);
});

    4. Memory Leaks from Un-Removed Listeners

    // ❌ If this element is repeatedly created/destroyed without removing its
// listener, each old listener + its closure stays in memory
function setup() {
    const el = document.createElement("div");
    el.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("clicked"));
    return el;
}

// ✅ Clean up listeners when an element/component is removed for good
el.removeEventListener("click", handler);

    INTERMEDIATE10. Best Practices

    1. Always Use addEventListener, Never on* Properties

    // ✅ Composable, doesn't silently overwrite
el.addEventListener("click", handler);

    2. Delegate Events for Dynamic Lists

    // ✅ One listener, works for present and future items
container.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    if (e.target.matches(".item")) handleItemClick(e.target);
});

    3. Store Handler References for Later Removal

    // ✅ Enables clean removal
const handler = () => console.log("clicked");
el.addEventListener("click", handler);
// later: el.removeEventListener("click", handler);

    4. Use { once: true } for One-Time Listeners

    // ✅ No manual cleanup needed
el.addEventListener("click", showTooltip, { once: true });

    5. Call preventDefault() Early in the Handler

    // ✅ Prevent the default action before anything else can go wrong
form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    // ... rest of the logic
});

    📋 Quick Reference Summary

    Concept Key Points
    addEventListener Registers handlers without overwriting existing ones; supports options like once/capture.
    Event object e.target (origin), e.currentTarget (listener's element), e.type, e.key.
    preventDefault() Cancels the browser's built-in default action (navigation, form submit/reload).
    Bubbling/Capturing Events travel down (capture) then up (bubble) through the DOM tree.
    stopPropagation() Stops the event from reaching ancestor listeners further along the path.
    Delegation One listener on a parent, checking e.target — scales to dynamic children.
